body.html: Amoebiasis is carriage of Entamoeba histolytica, with or without symptoms. It is strictly human (caecum and sigmoid-rectum), worldwide, linked to the faecal hazard, commoner in hot, humid, poorly sanitised regions, and the 3rd parasitic cause of death. 90% of infections are asymptomatic (amoebiasis-infection); 10% are symptomatic (amoebiasis-disease): intestinal (colon) and extra-intestinal (mainly liver, then lung). Of the 9 amoebae living in the human gut, only E. histolytica is pathogenic; E. dispar and E. moshkovskii look identical but are harmless, as are E. coli, E. hartmanni, Endolimax nana and others.

Three forms. Histolytica trophozoite: 20-40 µm, fast unidirectional pseudopods, nucleus with central karyosome and fine peripheral chromatin, ingests red cells (haematophagous): the invasive, pathogenic form causing necrosis. Minuta: 10-15 µm, non-haematophagous commensal of the colonic lumen in healthy carriers. Cyst: spherical 10-15 µm, 1 to 4 nuclei when mature, chromatoid bodies; the infective, resistant form: resists chlorine, killed by freezing (-5 °C) and above 40 °C.

Reservoir: humans (food handlers) and the environment. Faecal-oral: contaminated water, raw vegetables fertilised with human waste or sewage, dirty hands (cysts under nails); also oral-anal sexual contact. At risk: people in poor sanitary conditions, migrants, travellers, institutions, MSM; severe in children, elderly and pregnant women. Short direct (monoxenous) cycle: ingested cyst excysts into a 4-nucleate amoeba giving 8 trophozoites; in amoebiasis-infestation minuta forms live in the lumen and encyst, cysts leave in stool; in amoebiasis-disease they become histolytica forms whose lytic enzymes cause ulcers.

Acute intestinal amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery): incubation 1-4 weeks, sudden onset, severe abdominal pain, sometimes fever and vomiting; dysenteric syndrome: 10-15 stools/day of mucus and blood without faeces ('rectal sputum'), épreintes (colicky pain) and tenesmus. Hepatic amoebiasis: via the portal system, within 5 months of dysentery in 95%; pre-suppurative diffuse hepatitis or amoebic liver abscess: Fontan's triad (fever 39-40 °C, painful hepatomegaly, right upper quadrant pain), deterioration; 'anchovy-sauce' pus; a diagnostic and therapeutic emergency. Pulmonary amoebiasis: spread across the diaphragm, pleurisy, lung abscess, hepatobronchial fistula with chocolate-brown vomica. Rare: brain, skin, pericardium, spleen.

Intestinal → stool diagnosis: fresh stool, 3 exams a day apart; fresh exam for haematophagous trophozoites, Lugol, concentration for cysts; coproantigen ELISA. Visceral → serology: raised ESR and neutrophils, ELISA serology (diagnosis and follow-up; stays positive for months to years; ESR and neutrophils normalise in 4-6 weeks); imaging for abscess.

Treatment: tissue amoebicides (nitroimidazoles) that diffuse into tissues: metronidazole, ornidazole (1.5 g/day adult or 20-30 mg/kg/day for 10 days), tinidazole, secnidazole (2 g single dose); then a contact (luminal) amoebicide, active on minuta forms and cysts in the lumen: paromomycin (1.5 g/day adult, 50 mg/kg/day child; alternative intestinal antiseptics). Surgery or image-guided aspiration for large abscesses. Prevention: no vaccine or chemoprophylaxis; hand washing, washing fruit and vegetables, boiling or filtering water, sanitation, health education, early diagnosis.

Aspergilloses are diseases due to cosmopolitan, opportunistic filamentous fungi of the genus Aspergillus, whose conidia we inhale constantly. The spectrum goes from immunoallergic manifestations and localised colonisation (aspergilloma) to severe invasive multi-organ disease. Diagnosis is difficult and combines clinical, biological and radiological data.

Moulds with hyaline septate hyphae (hyalohyphomycetes); about 300 species: A. fumigatus (90%), A. flavus, A. nidulans, A. niger, emerging A. terreus. Aspergillary head: conidiophore → vesicle ± metulae → phialides → chains of conidia. The wall galactomannan is released into serum, BAL, CSF and urine and is used to diagnose invasive aspergillosis.

Reservoir: everywhere (air, soil, carpets, flowers, cereals, air conditioners, food such as pepper and herbal teas, water); humidity favours it; the 'aspergillary cloud' enters homes and hospitals. Contamination: inhalation of conidia; wounds, burns, surgical sites; food and water. Defences: skin barrier, mucociliary clearance, alveolar macrophages and neutrophils. Risk factors: construction works (outbreaks in haematology; protect with laminar flow and HEPA filters); local (damaged epithelium, pre-formed cavities such as tuberculosis, smoking, cystic fibrosis, radiotherapy); general: profound prolonged neutropenia (< 500/mm³), corticosteroids, hereditary NADPH-oxidase deficiency (chronic granulomatous disease).

Hypersensitivity: extrinsic allergic alveolitis (farmer's lung, mouldy hay or grain, pigeon feeding; type III/IV; cough, fever, dyspnoea 6-8 h after exposure, lasting 24-48 h; repeated attacks → interstitial fibrosis; anti-Aspergillus precipitins in non-atopic subjects); aspergillary asthma (type I; eosinophilia, specific IgE, positive skin tests); ABPA in asthma or cystic fibrosis (bronchial obstruction, productive cough, mucous plugs with Aspergillus, positive skin tests and precipitins, eosinophilia > 1000/mm³, raised total IgE). Aspergilloma: fungus ball in a pre-existing cavity communicating with a bronchus; imaging shows the air crescent ('bell') sign; haemoptysis. Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA): opportunistic, iatrogenic, nosocomial, high mortality; haematological malignancies, marrow and organ transplants, aplastic chemotherapy; main factor neutropenia < 500/mm³ for over 10 days, also steroids. Suspect it with fever resistant to broad-spectrum antibiotics for over 4 days in an immunocompromised patient; often pleuritic pain; CT: halo sign (perinodular haemorrhage), later air crescent. Extrapulmonary: otomycosis, keratitis after trauma, skin (burns), onyxis, sinusitis.

Aspergillus is ubiquitous: distinguish true infection from colonisation or contamination; no test is enough alone. International criteria classify IA as proven (tissue hyphae with damage, or culture from a sterile site), probable or possible, combining host, clinical and mycological criteria. Direct exam (septate hyphae; fast, cheap, insensitive), culture on Sabouraud-chloramphenicol at 37 °C in 3-4 days, identification by head and conidia morphology or MALDI-TOF. Serum galactomannan: twice-weekly screening during neutropenia; positive before cultures, imaging and symptoms; confirm on a second sample; false positives with piperacillin-tazobactam, amoxicillin-clavulanate and some foods. β-1,3-D-glucan: pan-fungal marker. Antibodies (WB, IEP, ELISA): useful in alveolitis, ABPA, aspergilloma. Histology (PAS, silver) up to 80% sensitive. CT: halo and air-crescent signs.

Antifungals: voriconazole (reference for IPA), other azoles (itraconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole), amphotericin B (liposomal), echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin); fluconazole and 5-FC are inactive; A. terreus resists amphotericin. Aspergilloma: surgery is the treatment of choice; local amphotericin paste or endocavitary instillation otherwise. Prevention: protective isolation in sterile rooms, HEPA filtration, strict hygiene during works; antifungal prophylaxis (posaconazole) in high-risk patients.

Schistosomiasis (bilharzia) is caused by blood flukes (schistosomes): separate-sex worms living in the venous plexuses. A disease of 'bare feet' and fresh water, with heavy morbidity, it spreads with irrigation and dams. Four species infect humans: S. haematobium (urogenital; snail Bulinus), S. mansoni (intestinal; Biomphalaria), S. japonicum (intestinal, with vascular complications; Oncomelania), S. intercalatum (rectal, genital; Bulinus).

Distribution depends on the snails and on human contact with fresh water: fishing, rice growing, irrigation; lack of wells (laundry, dishes in canals); ablutions and bathing; lack of latrines lets eggs reach the snails. In Morocco only urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium) exists: first cases 1927, south of the Atlas (Errachidia, Zagora, Agadir); the Ouarzazate dam extended irrigation and caused an outbreak; foci north of the Atlas (Marrakech, Beni Mellal, Kenitra, Tangier...).

Adults: unsegmented, two suckers; the whitish male folds into a gynaecophoric canal holding the thinner, darker female. Eggs: embryonated, spined: S. haematobium oval with a large terminal spine; S. mansoni oval with a large lateral spine; S. intercalatum rhomboid, terminal spine; S. japonicum round, small lateral spine. Heteroxenous cycle: eggs hatch in warm fresh water into a ciliated miracidium → snail → sporocysts → cercariae (the infective form) that penetrate the skin; schistosomules migrate (10-21 days) and mature (3 weeks). Some eggs cross into the bladder or bowel lumen and are excreted; others embolise to the liver, lungs and elsewhere, forming granulomas (epithelioid-giant cell, centred on egg debris) and fibrosis. Reservoir: humans (S. intercalatum), humans and animals for the others.

Penetration: within 30 min, lasting up to 2 days: cercarial dermatitis (papules, vesicles, itch), often discreet. Invasion (5-6 weeks): irregular fever, allergic signs (cough, asthma-like dyspnoea), fleeting oedema, headache, myalgia, diarrhoea, hepatosplenomegaly; very high eosinophilia; stool and urine exams are still negative; diagnosis by history and serology. State phase (egg laying): S. haematobium: terminal haematuria, cystitis, dysuria, frequency, cloudy bloody urine; genital fibrosis and sterility; bladder carcinoma. S. mansoni/japonicum: diarrhoea or bilharzial dysentery, abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, liver fibrosis and portal hypertension. S. intercalatum: proctitis.

Orientation: eosinophilia (up to 50% in the toxaemic phase, then 2-15%; rises again about day 15 of treatment), stay and fresh-water bathing in an endemic area; imaging: bladder calcifications on plain film (1/3), cystoscopy lesions (80%), urography (hydronephrosis), ultrasound; rectoscopy; urine dipstick for haematuria (used in control programmes). Parasitology (positive only 6-8 weeks after infection, impossible in invasion): urine for S. haematobium (circadian excretion peaking around noon, increased by exercise: collect urine after effort, end of micturition); stool with Kato (eggs per gram); live egg (moving miracidium, hatching test) = active disease, dead or calcified egg = old infection; rectal biopsy (Ziehl shell: negative for S. haematobium, positive for others), bladder biopsy. Serology (IFI, HAI, ELISA): positive 15-30 days after infection, so useful in the invasion phase, chronic phase and follow-up (rises after treatment, negative after 12-15 months). Treatment: praziquantel, single-day course: 40 mg/kg (haematobium, mansoni, intercalatum) or 60 mg/kg (japonicum); very well tolerated, used for mass treatment.

Candidiases are cosmopolitan infections due to yeasts of the genus Candida, arising when local or general immunity fails. They range from superficial mucocutaneous forms to deep or disseminated candidiasis, which remains serious despite modern antifungals.

Candida: budding yeasts, non-capsulated, non-pigmented, some forming pseudohyphae or true hyphae. C. albicans is the main pathogen and a normal commensal of the gut and natural cavities; others: C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, C. krusei, C. parapsilosis, C. dubliniensis, C. auris. Host factors: newborns, elderly (dentures), pregnancy; sweat, maceration, moisture, contact with sugar (pastry cooks), trauma; diabetes, neutropenia, cancer, HIV. Iatrogenic: antibiotics, corticosteroids, antiseptics, immunosuppressants, contraceptive hormones, radiotherapy, IV drug use, digestive or cardiac surgery, transplantation, IV catheters and parenteral nutrition, burns, urinary catheters, prostheses.

Oral: commensal becomes pathogen when flora is disturbed; risk factors: dentures, dry mouth (xerostomia), psychotropic drugs, inhaled steroids, antibiotics, chemo/radiotherapy, pregnancy, poorly controlled diabetes, undernutrition, HIV (CD4 < 300); thrush (pseudomembranous white plaques), heals without sequelae. Oesophageal: with oral candidiasis, common in HIV with CD4 < 100, cancer, leukaemia; dysphagia, retrosternal burning; endoscopy shows white-yellow plaques; biopsy. Digestive (rare, immunocompromised, anal involvement). Vulvovaginal: C. albicans 80%, C. glabrata 10%; 75% of women have one episode; pregnancy triggers; itch, burning, dyspareunia, dysuria, red swollen vulva, curd-like white discharge; balanitis in men. Skin: intertrigo of large folds (groin, abdomen, submammary, axillary, intergluteal) or small folds (lip commissures, finger webs): glazed, oozing erythema starting at the fold bottom with a white coating and satellite papulo-pustules; napkin candidiasis in infants. Nails: fingernails (3rd finger, dominant hand), favoured by water, sugar, manicure, diabetes; begins with painful perionyxis (pus on pressure) then onyxis.

Candidaemia, endophthalmitis, endocarditis, hepatosplenic, bone, cerebral, genitourinary candidiasis, pneumonia. Classified as proven (yeast on histology of a non-mucosal biopsy, or culture from a sterile site with compatible findings), probable or possible using host criteria (neutropenia < 500 for > 10 days, fever > 96 h despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, recent immunosuppressants or steroids > 3 weeks, AIDS), microbiological and clinical criteria (e.g. chorioretinitis). Mycological diagnosis is difficult: blood cultures, PCR, histology.

Sample by site (skin scales from the lesion edge, swabs, nail fragments, pus, stool, sputum after mouthwash, BAL, CSF, urine, blood cultures on fungal media, biopsies). Direct exam (essential, rapid): budding elements 1-10 µm, thin-walled, uncapsulated, ± filaments; in stool, sputum and mucosa only abnormal abundance means more than commensalism; count urine yeasts. Culture: Sabouraud-chloramphenicol (± actidione) at 25-37 °C for 3 days (1 week for deep samples); chromogenic media identify C. albicans directly. Identification of C. albicans: germ-tube (blastesis) test in serum at 37 °C for 3 h, latex agglutination (5 min), chlamydospores on RAT/PCB agar; other species by sugar assimilation (auxanogram) and fermentation, urease. Antifungigram (Etest). Serology: anti-Candida antibodies; mannan antigen and β-1,3-glucan; combined antigen + antibody suggests invasive candidiasis; follow-up is essential.

Oral: local amphotericin B suspension or mouthwash (15-21 days), nystatin, miconazole gel or mucoadhesive tablet; fluconazole 50 mg/day for 1-2 weeks if recurrent; treat the cause (dry mouth, clean and soak dentures). Cutaneous: local treatment alone (azoles, ciclopirox 4 weeks; terbinafine cream 2 weeks); avoid acidic soaps and alcohol antiseptics, dry the skin, treat other foci. Nails: local lotions + antiseptics, often systemic terbinafine 6 weeks or fluconazole; remove water/sugar/manicure factors. Disseminated: IV amphotericin B or lipid forms, fluconazole (IV then oral), voriconazole, echinocandins.

Coccidia are intracellular intestinal protozoa: Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora and Isospora. They develop in enterocytes in three phases: schizogony (asexual multiplication), gamogony (macro- and microgametes) and sporogony (oocyst passed in stool, the infective form). The pathogenic form is the intracellular trophozoite. They cause watery diarrhoea, self-limited in immunocompetent people (children especially) but severe and chronic in immunocompromised patients, above all in AIDS. The modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain reveals them. Blastocystis hominis is covered at the end.

Intracellular but extracytoplasmic parasite of intestinal (sometimes respiratory) microvilli; monoxenous. C. hominis (human) and C. parvum (humans and mammals); many mammals are reservoirs contaminating surface water. Oocysts resist chlorination → waterborne community epidemics; worldwide, especially developing countries; 2nd cause of infant diarrhoeal death in tropical areas. Oocyst: 4 sporozoites, infective when shed; transmission direct (hands, nurseries) or via water and food. Risk: AIDS with CD4 under 100/mm³, transplants; vets; children under 2. Clinical: secretory diarrhoea with malabsorption and villous atrophy. Immunocompetent: incubation 3-12 days, self-limited watery gastroenteritis for 1-2 weeks (children, travellers). Immunocompromised: severe, chronic, choleriform (up to 20 stools/day), resistant to treatment, spreading to bile ducts and lungs; death from fluid and nutritional loss. Diagnosis: stool with modified Ziehl-Neelsen (round pink oocysts), direct immunofluorescence (apple-green), coproantigen ELISA; duodenal aspirate, BAL, duodenal biopsy. Treatment: no reliably active drug; in AIDS, ART to restore immunity (CD4 > 500) with paromomycin, azithromycin or nitazoxanide (partial efficacy, relapses); immunocompetent patients heal spontaneously in under 2 weeks (nitazoxanide possible); rehydration and nutrition are essential.

Cyclospora cayetanensis: tropical (Central/South America, Africa, South-East Asia), small-intestine epithelium, strictly human, opportunistic; oocysts are shed immature and need maturation (long direct cycle); water and soiled produce (raspberries, strawberries, basil); watery traveller's diarrhoea (incubation 1-11 days; ~6 stools/day, cramps, bloating, fever, weight loss; chronic over 15 days in immunocompromised; may last up to 6 weeks). Modified ZN: orange-red oocysts. Treatment: cotrimoxazole twice daily for a week (in HIV four times daily for 10 days, then prophylaxis three times weekly); ciprofloxacin if intolerant.

Isospora belli: tropical, strictly human, opportunistic; faecal-oral; immature oocysts (long direct cycle); watery diarrhoea with fever 39-40 °C. Diagnosis: stool (3 samples every other day), duodenal fluid, BAL or biopsy; fresh exam and modified ZN. Treatment: symptomatic plus cotrimoxazole; alternatives ciprofloxacin, pyrimethamine with folinic acid.

Intestinal (colonic) protozoan, faecal-oral, worldwide, with vacuolar, granular, amoeboid and cystic forms; pathogenic mainly in the immunocompromised, children and the elderly; symptoms correlate with parasite numbers (more than 5 per field with diarrhoea): abdominal pain, watery diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, dehydration; chronic diarrhoea in HIV. Diagnosis by stool exam; treatment metronidazole, cotrimoxazole if it fails.

Cryptococcosis is a cosmopolitan mycosis due to an encapsulated yeast, Cryptococcus neoformans, of exogenous (environmental) origin, with tropism for the CNS: meningoencephalitis, plus lung, skin, bone and visceral forms. Defence relies on cellular immunity (CD4, CD8, NK), so it strikes the immunocompromised, above all AIDS with CD4 < 100/mm³ (an AIDS-defining illness).

C. neoformans (teleomorph Filobasidiella neoformans): varieties grubii and neoformans (serotypes A, D; cosmopolitan; soil, citrus, bird droppings) and gattii (B, C; tropical; eucalyptus, almond). Saprophytic in pigeon droppings and bat guano, resistant to drying. Round yeast 3-8 µm with a mucopolysaccharide capsule; grows at 37 °C on Sabouraud without actidione. Contamination by inhalation (latent primary lung infection), rarely skin inoculation; no human-to-human spread (except grafts). Risk: HIV (CD4 < 100): always test for HIV when cryptococcosis is found; long-term steroids, haematological malignancies, transplants, aplastic chemotherapy, sarcoidosis. Incidence peaked with AIDS (1985-95) and fell with ART.

Primary infection is pulmonary, then haematogenous spread with predilection for the CNS (CSF is a good culture medium and defences are weaker than in blood). Meningoencephalitis (80% of HIV+ cases, 60% of HIV−): sometimes silent, often insidious over weeks to months: moderate fever, headache, irritability, obtundation, cranial nerve palsies, then frank meningeal syndrome; severity: seizures, altered consciousness, motor deficit; raised intracranial pressure (papilloedema) needs evacuating punctures; a diagnostic and therapeutic emergency, fatal without treatment. Do a lumbar puncture whenever cryptococcosis is found elsewhere. Work-up: fundus, CT/MRI (mass, hydrocephalus), LP, extension (blood, urine, BAL, skin). Lung: usually silent; cough, fever, chest pain; nodules, infiltrates, pleurisy, nodes, cavitating mass. Skin: acneiform, pustular, nodular or ulcerated lesions on the face and limbs (in HIV: papule → umbilicated pustule → ulcer). Bone (flat bones, vertebrae) and disseminated forms (nodes, spleen, liver, marrow, prostate reservoir); fungaemia is a poor prognostic sign.

Finding the yeast is the only formal criterion; search in several sites. Emergency diagnosis: capsulated yeasts on India ink in the CSF centrifugation pellet plus cryptococcal antigen in CSF, BAL or serum. CSF: clear ('rock water'), high pressure, lymphocytic or mixed (10-100 cells), high protein, low glucose; may be normal in AIDS. India ink: the capsule appears as a clear halo. Culture: Sabouraud without actidione at 30 and 37 °C, 3-5 days (up to 3 weeks); mucoid, beige colonies; identification by capsule, growth at 37 °C, urease positive in 4 h. Serum antibodies are useless; capsular polysaccharide antigen (latex agglutination) in serum, CSF, BAL and urine is the method of choice, also for follow-up.

Meningitis in HIV+: amphotericin B (0.7-1 mg/kg/day) + flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day) for 2 weeks, then fluconazole 400 mg/day until week 10 (until cultures clear), then maintenance fluconazole 200-400 mg/day (stop with immune restoration); monitor renal and blood counts; lipid amphotericin if renal failure. Pneumonia: amphotericin if severe, otherwise fluconazole (HIV−: 200-400 mg/day for 6-12 months; HIV+: 400 mg/day). If Cryptococcus is found anywhere: extension work-up (LP with India ink, culture and antigen; urine; blood; lungs), look for poor prognostic signs, start treatment immediately, search for risk factors (HIV).

Parasitological diagnosis combines clinical and epidemiological context, eosinophil and IgE kinetics, and specific tests: the parasitological examination of stool (PES), blood examination, and immunological and molecular techniques. Each parasite is best detected by a technique adapted to it.

Three principles: a technique adapted to each parasite; one negative PES excludes nothing: prescribe 3 PES a few days apart; sampling quality is crucial. Preparation: 3-day low-residue diet (pasta, rice, eggs, dairy); stop charcoal, laxative oils, barium. Sampling: whole fresh stool in a clean, dry, sealed container, ideally collected in the lab; formed stools can wait up to 12 h, diarrhoeal stools within an hour (or MIF preservative); deliver in under 3 hours. Macroscopy: colour, consistency, blood, mucus, adult worms or fragments (tapeworm rings, pinworms, Ascaris). Microscopy: fresh exam; staining with Lugol (cysts yellow-brown, nuclei dark brown), ferric haematoxylin, MIF; concentration: physical (sedimentation or flotation, e.g. Willis with saturated NaCl; for helminth eggs, not protozoa) and diphasic (Bailenger, Ritchie: water/ether; eggs and cysts). Combine two concentration methods of different principle. Special: Ziehl-Neelsen (Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora: red oocysts on green), Kato (egg detection and count), Baermann (Strongyloides larvae, using thermo- and hygrotropism), Graham scotch test (pinworm).

Limits: parasites not shed in stool, eggs laid at the anus (pinworm), dead ends (larva migrans); false positives (starch, pollen, spores, leukocytes); time-consuming, expertise-dependent, low sensitivity. Coproantigen kits (immunochromatography under 30 min or ELISA) and PCR (sensitive, specific, multiplex, species identification) complement it.

Targets parasites living in blood or haematopoietic organs: intracellular (Plasmodium in red cells; Leishmania and Toxoplasma in leukocytes) and extracellular (microfilariae, trypanosomes). Sample from fingertip or heel, or venous blood on EDTA/citrate; timing matters: Plasmodium at fever peaks, microfilariae at 10-14 h or 22-24 h depending on periodicity. Fresh exam: mobile forms (trypanosomes, microfilariae). Thin smear (Giemsa, MGG, RAL 555; oil immersion ×100): reference for species identification and stage; parasitaemia as % of parasitised red cells. Thick drop: a concentration technique and the WHO reference for malaria. Leukoconcentration (microfilariae) and triple centrifugation (trypanosomes).

Antibody response depends on location: weak for strictly intestinal parasites (pinworm, flagellates), strong for tissue/blood parasites (Leishmania, filariae), variable for migrating parasites (Ascaris, Strongyloides). IgM early (under 10 days), no placental crossing; IgG a week later, plateau, long persistence, crosses the placenta; IgA local; IgE in helminthiases. Indications: when direct diagnosis is impossible (larval migration of Ascaris, hepatic amoebiasis, dead ends: larva migrans, hydatid cyst), post-treatment follow-up (hydatid cystectomy: transient rise then fall), congenital toxoplasmosis and immune status, antigen detection in invasive candidiasis, cryptococcosis and aspergillosis, epidemiology. Rules: at least two techniques (sensitive screening + specific confirmation) and two samples 15 days apart. Techniques: IFI (titre = highest positive dilution), ELISA (screening; toxoplasmosis, amoebiasis, aspergillosis), latex agglutination, and others.

Flukes (trematodes) are unsegmented, leaf-shaped flatworms with an incomplete gut (no anus) and two suckers (oral and ventral). Most are hermaphrodites with an indirect cycle requiring at least one intermediate host, a freshwater snail; they lay operculated, non-embryonated eggs. Humans are infected by mouth, eating encysted cercariae (metacercariae) on wild watercress or dandelion, or in raw fish, crabs or crayfish. The key disease here is fasciolosis (large liver fluke).

A zoonosis due to Fasciola hepatica, parasite of the bile ducts of sheep and cattle, humans being accidental hosts. Adults attach by suckers to the bile duct epithelium, feed on cells and blood, and lay eggs passed in faeces. The intermediate host is the freshwater snail Lymnaea truncatula (found 'under the cattle's hoof'); metacercariae encyst on wild watercress. Clinical: an invasion phase (weeks 1-4, up to 2 months): transhepatic migration of young flukes with toxi-infectious hepatitis; a state phase (from about 3 months): adults in the bile ducts → oedema, inflammation, epithelial hyperplasia, angiocholitis, obstruction, pseudolithiasis sometimes discovered at surgery.

Other hepatic flukes: Asian Opisthorchis viverrini and Clonorchis sinensis (Chinese fluke; raw freshwater fish); cosmopolitan Dicrocoelium dendriticum (small liver fluke of animals, via ants; eggs in human stool may be simple transit after eating infected liver). Lung flukes (Paragonimus): raw crabs or freshwater shrimp; mimic tuberculosis (haemoptysis, wasting; eggs in sputum). Intestinal flukes (Metagonimus, Heterophyes, Fasciolopsis buski) in Asia and Africa (Egypt): digestive disorders.

Parasitology: eggs in faeces, bile or sputum, positive only from about 3 months (state phase); concentration (flotation, Kato for counts); duodenal aspirate if stool is negative. F. hepatica egg: oval, yellow-brown, thin smooth shell, operculated, non-embryonated. Serology (IFI, IEP, ELISA): positive in over 90%, from 3 weeks, so useful in the invasion phase; after treatment titres first rise (antigen release), fall from week 5-6 and become negative in 7-12 months, allowing follow-up. Prevention: avoid wild watercress, water chestnuts and undercooked fish.

Flagellates are protozoa that move by flagella (sometimes an undulating membrane) and divide by binary fission. Several live in the human gut (Chilomastix mesnili, Trichomonas intestinalis, Enteromonas hominis, Embadomonas) and are well tolerated; only Giardia intestinalis is pathogenic in the gut (giardiasis). Trichomonas vaginalis causes a sexually transmitted genital infection.

Caused by Giardia intestinalis (G. lamblia, G. duodenalis), multiplying in the duodenum and jejunum; worldwide, commoner in hot humid areas, epidemic in communities; the commonest cause of non-bacterial diarrhoea, mostly in young children and nurseries. Trophozoite: pear-shaped, bilaterally symmetrical, 2 nuclei, 4 pairs of flagella, 'falling-leaf' movements. Cyst: oval, thick-walled, 4 nuclei, gives 2 trophozoites; resistant (including to bleach) and infective. Cycle: monoxenous (human), cysts ingested with water or food, excystation in the stomach, binary fission in the duodenum, cysts shed in stool; faecal hazard, family, nursery and retirement-home spread.

Pathophysiology: attachment to enterocytes of the duodenal and jejunal microvilli → villous atrophy, brush border destruction; the parasite consumes nutrients and captures bile acids → malabsorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins, B12 (anaemia). Clinical: 90% healthy carriers; incubation ~7 days; diarrhoea 5-10 stools/day, cramps, flatulence, vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, steatorrhoea, vitamin deficiencies, failure to thrive in children with foul, pale stools. Think of giardiasis in a child with diarrhoea over a week progressing in bouts. Diagnosis: 3 stool exams a day apart (saline, Lugol, concentration); duodenal aspirate or biopsy if negative with strong suspicion; coproantigens for follow-up and epidemiology. Treatment: metronidazole (750 mg/day adult; 25 mg/kg/day child for 5-7 days), or single-dose tinidazole or secnidazole 2 g; stool control 10 days later and repeat the course. Prevention: treat carriers, safe food and water (boil, filter, iodine), latrines.

Trichomonas vaginalis: strictly human, genital tract of both sexes, worldwide, sexually transmitted (newborns rarely, at birth). Trophozoite: pear-shaped, central nucleus, 4 anterior flagella and a posterior flagellum forming a short undulating membrane; motile, rotating clockwise; no cyst form. Women: vagina and urethra; alkaline pH favours it; onset often during or after menses; many are asymptomatic; symptomatic vaginitis: vulvar pruritus, frothy greenish-yellow foul-smelling discharge, burning, dysuria, dyspareunia; may coexist with Candida and gonococcus. Men: urethra and prostate; often latent or self-limited urethritis. Diagnosis: vaginal swab with speculum without lubricant; in men, morning urethral secretions before voiding (± prostate massage) or first-void urine sediment; fresh exam in saline (motile rotating parasite), Giemsa smear. Treatment: metronidazole 500 mg/day for 10 days (plus local tablets in women) or single-dose tinidazole/ornidazole 2 g; treat both partners; safe sex and hygiene.

Two small-intestine nematodes infect humans through the skin when bare feet or hands touch muddy soil contaminated by human faeces: the blood-sucking hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus), causing iron-deficiency anaemia, and Strongyloides stercoralis (anguillulosis), whose autoinfection cycle lets it persist for decades and explode into fatal malignant strongyloidiasis under corticosteroids.

A. duodenale (Old World): pinkish-white, 8-12 mm; buccal capsule with 2 pairs of hook-shaped teeth; female lays 15,000-20,000 eggs/day (50-60 µm, thin transparent shell, 2-4 blastomeres). N. americanus (New World): cutting plates; 5,000-10,000 eggs/day with about 8 blastomeres. Contamination: encysted infective L3 strongyloid larvae in warm, humid, faeces-enriched mud (mines), attracted by moisture and heat (positive hygro-, thermo- and histotropism); barefoot walking, farm work, gardening, miners. Cycle: eggs in faeces → rhabditoid L1 → strongyloid L2 → infective L3 → skin penetration → blood → heart → lungs → trachea → swallowed → duodenum (L4) → adult. Clinical: skin phase (erythema, dermatitis, pruritus; 'miner's itch' after repeated exposure), invasion phase (dry cough, dysphonia, Löffler syndrome, eosinophilia up to 50%), state phase (duodenal signs from blood-sucking adults, microcytic hypochromic iron-deficiency anaemia). Diagnosis: history (job, habitat), anaemia, eosinophilia; stool exam with Willis flotation and Kato egg count; coproculture showing larvae; adults after treatment or at endoscopy. Treatment: albendazole 400 mg single dose, mebendazole 200 mg/day × 3 days, pyrantel; iron and folic acid. Prevention: latrines, faecal-hazard control, worker screening (notifiable), boots, no barefoot walking in mud.

S. stercoralis: 1-2 mm; in the duodenum-jejunum only the parthenogenetic female (reproduces without a male); free-living males and females exist in soil. Larvae: rhabditoid (L1, double oesophageal bulb) and filariform/strongyloid L3 (single bulb, infective). Contamination: skin penetration by L3 (barefoot, muddy water); faecal hazard. Three cycles: indirect sexual (long, free-living generation in soil in favourable conditions), direct asexual (L1 in stool becomes infective L3 directly), and endogenous autoinfection (L1 become L3 inside the gut or at the anal margin without leaving the body), explaining persistence for 30 years or more.

Clinical: skin phase (pruritus, papular erythema), invasion (dry cough, asthma attacks, Löffler syndrome), state phase (abdominal pain, diarrhoea); larva currens: fast-moving, sinuous, erythematous cords around the belt and abdomen during autoinfection. Malignant (disseminated) strongyloidiasis: rare but severe in the immunocompromised, especially on long-term corticosteroids, lymphoma or transplants: larvae invade all organs and fluids (urine, CSF), with pulmonary and neurological complications and death. Orientation: origin, barefoot or farm work, very high eosinophilia (50-60%) in a 'saw-tooth' pattern (repeated autoinfection). Certainty: rhabditoid larvae in stool; Baermann method (hygro- and thermotropism) and coproculture, essential for light infections. Treatment: albendazole (3 days) or ivermectin 200 µg/kg single dose. Prevention: faecal control, high shoes in mud, latrines, screening and treating carriers (important before steroids).

Hydatidosis is a cosmopolitan, rural zoonosis: the development in humans and herbivores of the larva of a small tapeworm, Echinococcus granulosus, whose adult lives in the dog's intestine. It is a major public-health and economic problem in North Africa and Morocco (about 2% mortality among diagnosed cases; 15,000 to over 50,000 dirhams per patient). At-risk jobs: vets, farmers, butchers; stray dogs spread it.

Dog: main reservoir and definitive host (about one dog in two infected; first reason for seizure in slaughterhouses). Herbivores (sheep): intermediate hosts. Humans: accidental intermediate hosts (dead end). Humans are infected directly (licking, stroking dogs) or indirectly (water, fruit, vegetables contaminated by eggs). In the host, the hexacanth embryo crosses the gut wall and settles in the liver or other organs, forming a hydatid; a dog eating infected offal develops adult worms in 6 weeks. Why so endemic in Morocco: traditional pastoral and nomadic herding, 1-3 untreated dogs per herd, dead animals left unburied, millions of dogs (many stray), dogs at souk slaughterhouses, clandestine and family slaughter (weddings, Eid al-Adha, moussems) with offal given to dogs, poor hand and vegetable hygiene (children). Most affected regions (2010): Meknès-Tafilalet, Chaouia-Ouardigha, Doukkala-Abda.

Adult: 3-6 mm; scolex with 4 suckers and 2 rows of hooklets; short neck; strobila of 3 segments, the last full of eggs. Hydatid cyst = hydatid + pericyst. From outside in: pericyst (adventitia): host organ tissue compressed by the cyst, not parasitic; ectocyst (cuticle): white acellular outer wall; endocyst (germinal layer): thin fertile membrane producing brood capsules with protoscolices and secreting the hydatid fluid. Hydatid sand (free brood capsules, protoscolices, hooklets) settles at the bottom. Protoscolices released by cracking or rupture can seed secondary echinococcosis.

Long silent phase (mechanical effect only); 50% of state-phase cases are asymptomatic; one organ in 85-90%, a single cyst in 70%. Liver (50-60%): latency 10-15 years, painless hepatomegaly, pain, digestive signs, fever; complications: compression of bile ducts or vessels, cracking or rupture (immediate allergy up to anaphylactic shock; late secondary echinococcosis), infection (liver abscess), cholestatic jaundice. Lung (30-40%): shorter latency; cough, haemoptysis, vomica (rupture into a bronchus), dyspnoea, pleurisy; infection (lung abscess); 'water-lily' sign on imaging. Kidney (1.5-5%): mostly left; mass, pain, haematuria, hypertension, hydaturia. Others (~1%): bone (vertebrae), CNS, spleen, heart, muscle, orbit, thyroid, breast.

Definitive confirmation is on the surgical specimen. Orientation: origin, occupation, dog contact; eosinophilia (marked in invasion; normal or 7-15% in the state phase; rises with cracking, with IgE); neutrophilia = superinfection. Imaging: ultrasound is the key test and guides treatment, using the WHO-IWGE classification: CL, CE1 (simple unilocular), CE2 (multivesicular, 'honeycomb/rosette'), CE3 (detached membranes ± daughter cysts), CE4 (degenerative, 'ball of wool'), CE5 (calcified); chest X-ray, CT, MRI for number and size. Serology (a negative result does not exclude it, e.g. calcified cysts): screening with ELISA + haemagglutination (> 85%), confirmation by Western blot (17 kDa band specific to E. granulosus); follow-up by ELISA: titres rise 4-6 weeks after surgery then become negative in 12-24 months; persistence or reappearance suggests recurrence (control every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months). Direct: protoscolices, hooks or membranes in cyst fluid, vomica or urine; PCR.

Surgery cures ~90% (sterilise the cyst, remove the germinal membrane; radical pericystectomy or dome resection), with perioperative albendazole; contraindications: pregnancy, difficult access, multiple cysts. PAIR (Puncture, Aspiration, Injection of a scolicide such as 95% alcohol or hypertonic saline, Re-aspiration) under ultrasound with albendazole before and after; percutaneous drainage for large cysts. Albendazole alone for small (< 5 cm) or multiple cysts (adults 400 mg; children 15 mg/kg/day, max 800); side effects: neutropenia, raised transaminases, alopecia; contraindicated in the first trimester. Watch and wait for inactive CE4-CE5 cysts. By stage: CE1/CE3a ≤ 10 cm → PAIR; > 10 cm → drainage; CE2/CE3b → surgery; complicated cysts → drainage or surgery. Prevention: veterinary slaughter control, incinerate offal, no clandestine slaughter; keep dogs out of slaughterhouses and deworm dogs with praziquantel; hand washing, wash raw vegetables, keep dogs away from food; screening; a recombinant vaccine protects animals (95%).

A parasite is a eukaryotic infectious agent that, during its life cycle, develops temporarily or permanently at the expense of another eukaryotic living being, the host, harming it without necessarily killing it (unlike a predator). This distinguishes parasites from viruses (akaryotic) and bacteria (prokaryotic). Knowing each parasite's cycle and actors explains its pathophysiology and guides diagnosis, treatment and prevention.

Binomial names: Genus (capital) + species (lower case), in italics, e.g. Schistosoma mansoni. Two sub-kingdoms: Protozoa (unicellular; classified by morphology and locomotion): intestinal (Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia, Cryptosporidium), blood and tissue (Plasmodium, Toxoplasma, Trypanosoma, Leishmania), urogenital (Trichomonas vaginalis); Metazoa (multicellular): helminths: nematodes (roundworms: Ascaris), cestodes (flatworms: Taenia), trematodes (flukes: Schistosoma, Fasciola); and arthropods (external skeleton).

Parasitism ("who eats next door"): one benefits at the host's expense (E. histolytica causes ulcers and dysentery); it can be facultative (fly larvae in a wound), accidental (human for Echinococcus granulosus, whose definitive host is the dog), or obligate, temporary (tick) or permanent (louse). Commensalism ("who eats with"): benefits one, neutral for the other (Candida albicans, Entamoeba coli in the gut). Symbiosis/mutualism: both benefit (lichen; flagellates in termites). Parasitic dead end: infective form in an unusual host that never reaches adulthood but may cause disease (larva migrans).

Types: anthroponosis (humans only: ascariasis, amoebiasis, pinworm), anthropozoonosis (mainly animals: trichinosis, hydatid cyst), zoo-anthroponosis (mainly humans, animals in the cycle: taeniasis). Ectoparasites live on the surface (ticks, lice: infestation); endoparasites inside (hollow organs, tissues, cells: infection).

Habitats: small and large intestine, blood vessels, organs (liver, lung, heart, brain), muscles, lymphatics, reticulo-endothelial system, red cells. Sources: water, soil, raw vegetables and fruit, animals, fish, arthropod vectors, blood. Entry: direct contact (ectoparasites), ingestion (amoebae, helminth eggs), inhalation (fungal spores), trans-cutaneous (Schistosoma in fresh water), sexual (Trichomonas), transplacental (Toxoplasma), insect bite (Plasmodium). Exit decides the test: faeces (stool exam), urine (urinary schistosomiasis), sputum, or none (dead end: trichinosis, muscle biopsy). Harm: toxic products (allergy, necrosis), anaemia (malaria, Ancylostoma), weight loss (Giardia), fever and eosinophilia (roundworms), obstruction (Ascaris), compression (hydatid cyst), abortion and malformations (T. gondii).

A parasitic cycle is the obligatory sequence of transformations from one generation's egg to the next. Definitive host: adult or sexual forms. Intermediate host: larval or asexual forms. Vector: usually an insect that actively transmits (as HI: Chrysops for Loa loa; as HD: Anopheles for malaria). Reservoir: keeps the parasite in nature: humans only (ascariasis), animals and humans (leishmaniasis), animals only (hydatid cyst). Cycles: short direct (monoxenous, no outside maturation: amoebae), long direct (maturation in the environment: Ancylostoma), indirect (heteroxenous: Taenia with pig or cattle; filariae with a vector), dead end (dog hookworm larvae in human skin).

Example, pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis): human reservoir and host, no HI or vector, cosmopolitan; embryonated eggs ingested or inhaled from hands, bedding, air; adults in 2-4 weeks; evening anal pruritus; Graham scotch-tape test; albendazole repeated 15-21 days later plus treating the household, hand washing, cutting nails, washing bedding (auto-infestation).

Contributing factors: transmission route, climate and vector ecology (malaria, leishmaniasis, bilharzia), occupation (breeders, butchers: hydatid cyst), eating habits (raw meat and fish, aquatic plants; T. gondii cysts destroyed above 65 °C), hygiene and the faecal hazard, resistant forms (Cryptosporidium oocysts in water).

Leishmaniases are anthropozoonoses caused by flagellate protozoa of the genus Leishmania, obligate intracellular parasites of the mononuclear phagocyte system, transmitted by the sandfly (Phlebotomus). A WHO priority disease: 350 million at risk, 12 million cases, 2 million new cases a year. Notifiable in Morocco since 1995; cutaneous scars carry social stigma. Three clinical forms: visceral, cutaneous, mucocutaneous.

Dimorphic, heteroxenous: promastigote (15-25 µm, flagellated, motile) in the sandfly gut and culture; amastigote (2-6 µm, aflagellate, intracellular) in mammals; binary fission. Vector: small (2-5 mm) hairy yellowish sandfly, hunched, wings raised in a V, active at dusk and night above 19 °C, silent short flight, painful bite; larvae in damp soil, burrows. Reservoirs: dog (L. infantum), rodents (L. major), humans (L. tropica, L. donovani). Cycle: the sandfly ingests infected macrophages; promastigotes multiply in its gut and move to the proboscis; at the next bite they are injected, phagocytosed by macrophages and become amastigotes. Distribution: visceral L. infantum (Mediterranean), L. donovani (India, East Africa); cutaneous L. major (arid Maghreb), L. tropica (some foci in Morocco), L. infantum; New World species (L. braziliensis, mexicana, guyanensis, amazonensis).

Kala-azar ('black fever'). Zoonotic VL (L. infantum), classically in young children around the Mediterranean; anthroponotic VL (L. donovani) at all ages with dark skin macules. Incubation 3-6 months (up to years); often asymptomatic. Triad: irregular fever, pallor, splenomegaly, with hepatomegaly, lymph nodes, weight loss, digestive signs, bleeding (epistaxis, gum), skin and renal involvement; fatal without treatment, good outcome if treated early. Adults: incomplete triad, CD4 immunosuppression. Biology: aregenerative normochromic anaemia, leukoneutropenia, thrombocytopenia (pancytopenia); polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, ESR 80-100. Parasitology: amastigotes on MGG in bone marrow (sternal puncture in adults, iliac crest in children), lymph node, or blood in immunocompromised; NNN culture. Serology: ELISA, Western blot (14 and 16 kD bands), rK39 rapid test (sensitivity > 90%). PCR for follow-up. HIV co-infection (CD4 < 200): atypical, disseminated forms.

Old World localised: L. tropica (anthroponotic, urban, 'dry'): incubation 20 days-7 months, usually a single lesion on exposed skin; papule → central ulcer with crust and inflamed border; painless; slow (over a year), unsightly scar. L. major (zoonotic, rural, 'wet'): short incubation 10-45 days, multiple inflamed crater lesions, heals in under 6 months with a large scar. L. infantum: single nodule on the face without ulcer. New World: more chronic and mutilating (chiclero's ulcer, uta, pian bois). Diffuse cutaneous (L. aethiopica, mexicana, amazonensis): non-ulcerated nodules, generalising, treatment-resistant; differential: leprosy. Post-kala-azar dermal (L. donovani). Mucocutaneous (espundia, L. braziliensis): destruction of nose, palate, pharynx, larynx; death from malnutrition and pneumonia.

Diagnosis: presumption (painless ulcer on exposed skin, stay in endemic area, chronicity, antibiotic failure); certainty: scraping or dermal juice from the lesion edge, MGG smear (≥ 2 amastigotes with nucleus and kinetoplast), NNN culture (22-25 °C, 14 days), biopsy.

Cutaneous: clean with soap and water; single small lesion: watchful waiting ± antiseptic/antibiotic for superinfection. Pentavalent antimony (Glucantime, meglumine antimoniate): intralesional twice weekly for 3-4 weeks (Morocco: under 5 lesions, under 4 cm) or IM 20 mg/kg/day (more than 5 lesions or over 4 cm). Others: topical paromomycin (L. major), fluconazole, miltefosine, liposomal amphotericin B, thermotherapy (50 °C for 30 s) and cryotherapy. Glucantime contraindications: age over 50, pregnancy, severe renal, hepatic or cardiac failure. Visceral: meglumine antimoniate 60 mg/kg/day IM for 28 days; relapse: amphotericin B; liposomal amphotericin B 3 mg/kg/day for 5 days + day 10 (or 10 mg/kg for 2 days). Monitor antimony toxicity: ECG (QT prolongation, T and ST changes, arrhythmias), blood counts, liver, pancreas, kidney.

Malaria ('bad air', swamp fever) is caused by protozoa of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito; it is the most important parasitic infectious disease worldwide. Three actors: the parasite, the human reservoir (no innate immunity; acquired premunition builds over about 5 years and is lost in 1-2 years away from exposure) and the vector (bites at night, 11 p.m.-4 a.m., breeds in fresh stagnant water). Any fever in someone returning from an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise.

WHO 2021: 3.2 billion at risk, 93 countries, 241 million cases (95% in Africa) and 627,000 deaths, 90% of deaths in Africa, 65% in children under 5; P. falciparum in 99%; insecticide resistance and artemisinin resistance are spreading. Morocco: national programme from 1965, last indigenous case 2004, WHO certification of elimination in 2010; today cases are imported, and the goal is to prevent reintroduction.

Five species: P. falciparum (malignant tertian, 48 h; the most dangerous: cerebral malaria; no relapse beyond 2 months after return), P. vivax and P. ovale (benign tertian, 48 h; late relapses from hepatic hypnozoites), P. malariae (benign quartan, 72 h; recrudescence for years), P. knowlesi (South-East Asia, macaque reservoir, 24-h fever, possible severe forms; refer to a reference centre). Transmission: Anopheles bite, and also transfusion, transplant, congenital, needlestick, 'airport' malaria. Heteroxenous cycle: in humans (asexual) a liver phase then the erythrocytic cycle (ring → trophozoite → schizont → merozoites; synchronous rupture causes the fever paroxysm); in the mosquito, the sexual (sporogonic) cycle.

Uncomplicated primary attack (90%): incubation 7-21 days; fever, chills and sweats, headache, myalgia, digestive signs; biology: haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia. Severe malaria (P. falciparum): cytoadherence and sequestration of schizont-infected red cells in brain and organ capillaries → hypoxia. WHO criteria include coma (Glasgow ≤ 9), repeated seizures, Hb under 7 g/dL, hypoglycaemia, acidosis (bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L), respiratory distress, renal failure, haemoglobinuria, DIC, pulmonary oedema, jaundice, hyperlactataemia, parasitaemia ≥ 4%; mortality 10-25%: a diagnostic and therapeutic emergency. Other forms: evolutive visceral malaria, hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly, blackwater fever, quartan nephritis.

A biological emergency: results within 2 hours. Questions: Plasmodium present? which species and stage? parasitaemia? Thin smear (species, stage, parasitaemia; ~100-200 p/µL) and thick drop (more sensitive, 5-20 p/µL; WHO reference) on EDTA blood; clues: red cell size and shape, Schüffner dots (vivax, ovale), Maurer's clefts (falciparum), rings, schizonts, gametocytes. Rapid diagnostic tests (HRP2 for falciparum; pLDH, aldolase) in 15 min, never used alone. PCR: most sensitive (0.005-1 p/µL), species and mixed infections, but no stage or quantification and positive for > 30 days after cure. Serology is not diagnostic (blood donors, epidemiology, visceral forms).

Morocco protocol, uncomplicated: P. falciparum: artemether-lumefantrine for 3 days + a single dose of primaquine 0.25 mg/kg; P. vivax/ovale: chloroquine + primaquine (to eradicate hypnozoites; check G6PD); P. malariae: chloroquine. Severe/cerebral malaria: intensive care, IV artesunate (or IV quinine); monitor parasitaemia (72 h < 25% of initial, D7 and D28 negative), CBC, glucose, ECG. Gametocytes after treatment do not justify retreatment. Prevention: treat and use chemoprophylaxis; avoid bites (repellents, long clothing, insecticide-treated nets); vector control (breeding sites, insecticides, surveillance).

Malassezioses are benign, frequent but recurrent skin mycoses due to overgrowth of Malassezia, lipophilic, keratinophilic commensal yeasts of sebaceous skin. Four pictures: pityriasis versicolor, dandruff (pityriasis capitis), seborrhoeic dermatitis and folliculitis.

Cosmopolitan, among the commonest mycoses, especially in tropical climates and in summer in temperate ones. Habitat: the pilosebaceous follicle; growth needs free fatty acids (lipase releases them from sebum), so colonisation rises at puberty and falls in old age; peak 18-40 years. Favouring factors: oils, moisturisers, fatty sunscreens and cosmetics; sweating (sauna, hammam, intense sport), summer; hormonal changes: Cushing's, pregnancy, contraceptives, corticosteroid therapy.

Pityriasis capitis: non-inflammatory scalp hyperkeratosis, little itch, dandruff, no hair loss. Seborrhoeic dermatitis: adolescents, adults, infants; erythematous-scaly ± itchy lesions on nasolabial folds, eyebrows, glabella, ears, sometimes the chest. Pityrosporum folliculitis: itchy follicular papules and pustules on the back and shoulders; favoured by sun, systemic steroids, cyclins. Pityriasis versicolor: benign but recurrent, young adults (20-25), an aesthetic problem; the colour of spots 'varies' with skin pigmentation. Lesion: round well-limited macule of a few mm, starting around a hair follicle and growing centrifugally, merging into large polycyclic sheets; colour pink-buff to 'café au lait', later achromic; always finely scaly, revealed by scratching ('chip' sign, signe du copeau). Sites: sebaceous areas (trunk, root of limbs, submammary, scalp); in the tropics also arms, neck, face, abdomen, thighs.

Malassezia: small (3-6 µm) round to cylindrical, lipid-dependent, urease-positive yeasts. Wood's lamp: yellow-green fluorescence. Scotch-tape test or scale scraping stained with 2% methylene blue: clusters of round to oval spores (3-5 µm) with a double contour ('bunch of grapes') and short, stocky filaments; some yeasts with a unipolar bud ('bottle' shape). Culture is not needed.

Explain that it is mild, merely unsightly, due to a normal skin fungus, not contagious ('not caught on beaches'), and prone to relapse; hypopigmentation persists after cure but recolours over months (faster with sun). Local treatment suffices in localised forms: imidazoles (bifonazole, clotrimazole, econazole, ketoconazole, miconazole...), ciclopirox, terbinafine, tolnaftate, twice daily for 2-3 weeks; ketoconazole foaming gel single application; selenium sulphide; zinc pyrithione shampoo. Systemic for diffuse or recurrent forms: ketoconazole 200 mg/day for 10 days, fluconazole 300 mg/week for 2 weeks, itraconazole 200 mg/day for 5-7 days; UVA sessions.

Three intestinal nematodes (roundworms) spread by the faecal-oral route: pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis), roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides) and whipworm (Trichuris trichiura). The key difference is whether eggs are infective at laying (pinworm: short cycle, self-reinfection) or must mature in soil (Ascaris, whipworm: long cycle, 'dirty hands' and faecal-hazard diseases).

E. vermicularis: humans are the only reservoir; cosmopolitan; spread by close living (schoolchildren, elderly, institutions). Adults in the caecum and appendix: small, white, mobile; male 3-5 mm, female 9-12 mm. Each female lays 5,000-15,000 eggs a day at the perianal area at night. Eggs: elongated ovoid, flattened on one side, thin smooth shell, embryonated at laying. Short direct cycle, no tissue migration, adults in 2-4 weeks, longevity 1-2 months; eggs from hands, objects, linen, bedding and air are ingested or inhaled; autoinfestation. Clinical: evening anal pruritus, nausea, colic, insomnia, irritability; rarely appendicitis, vulvitis. Diagnosis: Graham scotch-tape test. Treatment: albendazole, repeated 15-21 days later, treat the household, wash hands, cut nails, wash pyjamas and bedding, vacuum.

A. lumbricoides: large adults (female 20-35 cm with a straight tail, male 15-30 cm with a curved tail), very mobile, in the small intestine; 200,000 eggs per female per day. Eggs: ovoid, double shell with a brown mamillated outer coat, not embryonated at laying; they mature in soil in 1-12 months. Long direct cycle with tissue migration: ingested embryonated eggs (water, food soiled by faeces) release larvae that migrate through the liver and lungs before returning to the gut; adults in 8-12 weeks, longevity about a year; no autoinfestation. Migration phase: Löffler syndrome (cough, fever, ± urticaria, transient lung infiltrate), high eosinophilia (Lavier curve). State phase: diarrhoea, abdominal pain, vomiting; rare surgical complications (occlusion, peritonitis) due to the worm's size and mobility. Diagnosis: eggs on stool exam, or a worm passed spontaneously. Treatment: albendazole or mebendazole, plus faecal-hazard control.

T. trichiura: human reservoir, cosmopolitan; pinkish-white worm, thin anterior two thirds and thick posterior third (whip shape); male tail coiled, female straight. Eggs lemon-shaped with a mucous plug at each pole, double shell, not embryonated at laying, maturing in soil. Long direct cycle; infection by embryonated eggs in water, raw vegetables or on hands. Clinical: invasion usually silent; colic, diarrhoea or constipation, nausea, anorexia, weight loss, irritability; heavy infection: profuse diarrhoea, tenesmus, rectal bleeding, rectal prolapse, appendicitis, hypochromic iron-deficiency anaemia. Diagnosis: stool exam.

Pneumocystosis is an opportunistic pneumonia due to the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii. It was the first complication of AIDS before triple therapy (CD4 < 200/mm³), led to the discovery of the AIDS epidemic, and remains a leading cause of ICU admission in HIV patients. Humans are the reservoir; transmission is airborne; the fungus multiplies in the alveoli, causing severe pneumonia.
HIV with CD4 < 200/mm³; also cancers, haemopathies, severe malnutrition, prematurity, T-cell deficiency, corticosteroids, chemotherapy and immunosuppressants (transplants).

An alveolar-interstitial lung disease in an immunocompromised patient that does not improve with conventional antibiotics. Symptoms: dyspnoea, dry cough, fever, weight loss, hypoxaemia (SaO₂ < 90%); insidious in HIV, faster in non-HIV patients. Auscultation is often normal. Chest X-ray: bilateral alveolar-interstitial syndrome; CT: ground-glass appearance.

Orientation: normal ESR and blood count (apart from HIV changes), low total lymphocytes, hypoxia ± respiratory alkalosis on blood gas, raised LDH, CD4 < 200. Certainty: the fungus cannot be cultured, so it must be seen directly in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), tracheal or bronchial aspirates or biopsies, with MGG or Grocott silver staining, or detected by PCR.

Curative, first line: cotrimoxazole (sulfamethoxazole 75 mg/kg/day + trimethoprim 15 mg/kg/day) for 21 days, IV or oral; side effects: rash, hepatitis, hyperkalaemia, renal failure, neutropenia, anaemia. Alternatives: atovaquone (if PaO₂ > 60 mmHg), pentamidine IV or aerosols. Corticosteroids if PaO₂ < 70 mmHg (reduce mortality and need for ventilation; US and French schedules over 21 and 9 days), oxygen, ventilation if needed, nutrition. Prophylaxis: cotrimoxazole one tablet daily (alternatives dapsone + pyrimethamine, monthly pentamidine aerosols, atovaquone). Primary: HIV with CD4 < 200; non-HIV at-risk patients (6 months after transplant, rejection). Secondary: after any episode, whatever the CD4. Stop when CD4 > 200 for at least 3 months on ART.

Toxoplasmosis is a worldwide zoonosis caused by Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular coccidian of warm-blooded animals with a preference for reticulo-endothelial cells. Usually asymptomatic and benign, it matters in two groups: non-immune pregnant women (congenital toxoplasmosis) and immunocompromised patients.

Crescent-shaped, apical complex at the pointed end. Three forms: tachyzoite (active intracellular multiplication by endodyogeny in the acute phase; spreads by blood and lymph; crosses the placenta); tissue cyst with bradyzoites (chronic phase in brain, muscle, heart, eye; out of reach of antibodies and drugs; persists for years; reactivates in immunodeficiency; destroyed by 50 °C for 30 min or −20 °C for 24 h); oocyst (only in cats and felines; shed in faeces, not infective when fresh; sporulates in soil and survives about a year). Definitive hosts: cats (sexual + asexual cycle); intermediate hosts: humans, birds, livestock (asexual only); humans are a dead end. Human infection: eating cysts in raw or undercooked meat; oocysts in water, raw vegetables or cat faeces; transplacental tachyzoites; organ transplant (cysts); transfusion; accidents. Fetal risk: in the first trimester transmission is rare but damage severe; in the third trimester transmission is frequent but lesions mild.

Immunocompetent: 80% asymptomatic; 15-20% benign illness with cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, asthenia, myalgia, healing without sequelae; mononucleosis syndrome. Congenital: early maternal infection may cause abortion; at term: severe form (hydrocephalus or microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, seizures, chorioretinitis, blindness, deafness, mental retardation), benign form (attenuated eye and brain signs, microphthalmia, cataract, jaundice, petechiae), latent form (80%) with later hydrocephalus, delay or chorioretinitis. Immunocompromised (acquired or reactivation, above all AIDS): toxoplasmic encephalitis with focal lesions (motor deficit, altered mental state, speech and movement disorders, cranial nerve palsies), ocular forms, disseminated fatal forms.

Serology uses two isotypes: IgG titration and IgM detection (ELISA, ISAGA), in the same laboratory throughout pregnancy. IgG+ IgM−: immune, old infection, no congenital risk. IgG− IgM−: non-immune: hygiene advice and monthly serology until after delivery. Seroconversion (IgM then IgG appear): antenatal and neonatal diagnosis. IgG+ IgM+: recent or residual IgM → IgG avidity (index > 0.5: infection over 4 months old; < 0.4: under 4 months) or a second sample at 3 weeks (rising titre = recent). In Morocco toxoplasmosis serology is part of pregnancy follow-up (2005 order) but not mandatory before marriage. Advice for seronegative women: well-cooked or previously frozen meat, wash fruit and vegetables, wash hands, avoid cat litter; no vaccine.

title: Diagnosis of congenital and immunocompromised forms, and treatment
subject: subj:parasito

body.html:
Antenatal: fetal ultrasound and PCR on amniotic fluid (amniocentesis from 14-20 weeks; sensitivity 60-70%). Neonatal: placenta, cord and infant blood; infant IgM (from day 5) = congenital infection; mother-infant Western blot comparison; follow-up for a year (maternal IgG should disappear). Immunocompromised: direct detection (MGG) or PCR in blood, CSF, BAL, marrow, biopsy.

Treatment: pregnant woman with seroconversion: spiramycin if antenatal diagnosis is negative; pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine if positive. Newborn: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid for 1 year (± steroids for chorioretinitis). AIDS: primary prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole if CD4 < 100 and seropositive (alternative dapsone-pyrimethamine), stopped when CD4 > 200 for 3 months on ART. Ocular: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine or clindamycin for 1 month.
